transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, honestly, I just... I can't seem to stop my brain from spinning, like, all the time. I came in because my mind is constantly jumping from one disaster to the next. Like right now, at work—I'm a chemist, well, an assistant in a materials lab, I only have some college so far—and there's this new partnership the lab just signed, and I just keep obsessing over whether they're going to cut my position to save money. And if they don't do that, I start panicking that maybe my data from last week's trials are wrong and they'll fire me for that instead. And then, you know, if I lose my job, my bills are going to pile up, and I won't be able to pay rent, and then I start thinking about how my family already probably thinks I'm falling behind because I haven't finished my degree yet. And then that just spirals into this whole thing about whether I've already completely ruined my chances at ever getting into grad school because I'm taking too long, and... it just never stops. It's exhausting. I just can't turn it off.
Do you find yourself especially anxious in certain social situations, like speaking in front of others or interacting with people in a group?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, it's not the people part that gets to me. I actually have to talk in front of the team at the lab pretty regularly, like when we have our weekly bench meetings every Tuesday morning. My supervisor always makes us go around the table and give updates on our material yields and testing phases. And I don't get nervous about the *speaking* part, or being in a group. I can talk to people just fine, I'm not scared they're judging my personality or how I talk or anything. 

But... I *do* worry the whole time I'm talking that the data I'm presenting is going to be the thing that gets me fired, like I mentioned before. So I'm anxious *in* the meeting, but not *because* it's a social situation, if that makes sense? 

Like, even outside of work, last weekend I went to a buddy's birthday dinner. There were maybe ten, twelve people there, some I didn't even know, and I wasn't anxious about talking to the new people at all. We actually had a really good conversation about some stuff. But the whole time I was sitting there, I was just obsessing in the back of my head about whether I was spending too much money on the dinner and how that's going to affect my rent, and if I was wasting time being there when I should be figuring out how to get back to classes and finish my degree. So, yeah, being around people is fine, I can do groups and all that, it's just that my brain is still running a million miles an hour about all my other problems while I'm doing it.
When you're feeling this constant worry or anxiety, do you notice any physical symptoms, like a racing heart, sweating, stomach issues, or trouble sleeping?

Well, physically... I don't know, I guess I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, I don't get sweaty or have a racing heart or anything like that. When I'm spiraling about work, or my degree, or the rent, it's really just all up in my head, you know? Like, my brain is just going and going and going, but my body feels... fine, I suppose. 

I mean, I don't have stomach issues, at least not that I can tie to the worry. Sometimes I'll eat something that doesn't agree with me, like the other day I had this spicy takeout from that place down the street from the lab—my coworker insisted we go there for lunch, even though I usually just bring a sandwich because, again, I'm trying to save money because of the whole rent and job security thing—and my stomach was a little off after that, but that was definitely the food, not the anxiety. 

And as for sleeping... I mean, I sleep okay, I guess. I don't have trouble falling asleep, or at least I don't think I do. It's more that when I'm awake, I'm just constantly thinking. But once I'm actually asleep, I'm out. I don't wake up in a panic or anything. So, yeah, no racing heart, no sweating, no stomach stuff, and sleep is fine. It's really just the thoughts. Just the constant, never-ending thoughts about everything that could go wrong.
Do you find yourself doing anything over and over again, like checking things, counting, or following certain routines, even if you don't really want to?

No, I don't really do anything like that. I mean, I don't have to count things or tap things or, like, check the stove a million times before I leave the apartment. It's funny you mention checking, though, because my roommate—he's this guy I met through a mutual friend a couple of years ago, great guy, but he's super particular about the apartment—he's always checking the locks and the windows, and sometimes he gets on my case if I don't double-check the deadbolt. But I don't feel compelled to do it, you know? I just do it to keep him happy so we don't get into an argument, because if we argue, then I start worrying that he's going to want to move out, and if he moves out, I'm stuck with the full rent, and like I said before, I'm already stressed enough about the rent and my job at the lab. 

But as for me, personally, doing things over and over... no. Like at work, I run my tests, I record the data, and I'm done. I don't have to go back and re-read the numbers ten times just to be sure, even though I'm terrified the numbers are wrong and I'll get fired. I just sit there and worry about it. I don't have any rituals or routines I have to follow. I don't have to wash my hands a certain way or organize my desk perfectly. Actually, my desk at the lab is kind of a mess right now because we've been running so many samples for this new partnership, and I just haven't had the time to clear away the old vials. So, yeah, no counting or checking or anything like that. It's really just the thoughts. The worrying is the only thing that's on repeat, just looping in my head all day long.

Have you ever had sudden episodes where you feel intense fear or discomfort that comes on very quickly, like your heart racing, feeling short of breath, or thinking something terrible is going to happen right then and there?

No, I haven't ever had anything like that. Like a sudden panic attack or something? No, it's never like a sudden burst of fear where I think I'm having a heart attack or can't breathe. It's more of a slow, constant burn, I guess you could say. 

Like, I don't suddenly feel like something terrible is going to happen right *that second*. It's more like I know something terrible is going to happen eventually, down the line, and I just can't stop thinking about it. Like with the lab, right? I don't suddenly think, "Oh my God, the building is exploding right now." It's more like, "I probably messed up that yield calculation yesterday, and when they review the quarterly reports next month, they're going to see it, and then they'll call me into the office, and then I'll be fired, and then I won't make rent, and then my roommate will kick me out." It's this whole long chain of events that I just sit there and chew on all day. 

I've never had a moment where my heart just starts pounding out of nowhere or I feel like I'm suffocating. Even when the worry gets really loud, like when I'm trying to figure out how to re-enroll in classes and I'm looking at the tuition costs, I don't get short of breath. I just get this heavy, sinking feeling that I'm never going to figure it out and I'm going to be stuck as a lab tech forever without my degree. But no sudden, intense episodes like you're talking about. It's just a constant hum of worry in the background, all the time, every day. It never really spikes into a sudden panic, it just... stays there. Always.
Have you ever worried that you might experience physical symptoms like a racing heart or shortness of breath, even if they haven’t actually happened to you?

No, I can't say I've ever worried about that happening. Like I was saying, the physical stuff just isn't part of it for me. I don't sit around thinking, "What if my heart starts racing?" or "What if I can't breathe?" because it's never happened, so it's not even on my radar as a possibility. My worries are always tied to real, concrete things that could actually ruin my life, you know? 

Like, I don't worry about my body failing me in that specific way. I worry about my bank account failing me. I worry about my career stalling out because I'm 24 and still just a tech with some college credits that are getting older by the minute. I worry about that new partnership at the lab and whether they're going to downsize the junior staff if the numbers don't look good for Q3. I mean, they had this whole meeting last week where the lab director was talking about "streamlining operations," and of course, my brain immediately goes to, "Well, I'm the one who hasn't finished his degree, so I'm the easiest one to cut." 

So, no, I don't worry about suddenly gasping for air or having my heart beat out of my chest. I'm too busy worrying about how I'm going to pay my half of the rent if "streamlining" means I'm out of a job. The anxiety is entirely focused on the external stuff—the job, the money, the school, the roommate situation. It's never about the anxiety itself causing some kind of physical meltdown. It's just the endless loop of "what ifs" about my future.
Do you ever feel especially anxious when you're being evaluated or when your performance is being judged, even if it's not about being socially embarrassed?

No, not really. I mean, I don't get a special, separate kind of anxious just because someone is watching me or grading me. It's not about the performance or the judgment itself, you know? 

Like, we have these quarterly performance reviews at the lab, and my supervisor will sit down with me and go over my error rates and my sample processing times. And sure, I'm worried during it, but it's not because he's looking at me or judging my worth as a chemist. I don't get stage fright. I'm not sitting there embarrassed or feeling like I'm on the spot. It's exactly what I was saying before—I'm just terrified that the review is the moment they decide to let me go. 

I've been a lab tech there for a couple of years now, ever since I had to pause my degree, and I actually know how to do the work. I know how to run the mass spec, I know how to prep the samples, I know the protocols inside and out. So when someone watches me work, I don't get performance anxiety. I don't get the shakes or forget what I'm doing. 

Just last month, actually, we had an external auditor come in to check our compliance for that new partnership I mentioned, and she was literally standing right over my shoulder with a clipboard while I was calibrating the equipment. And I wasn't sweating because she was evaluating me. I was just sitting there thinking, "If this calibration is off by even a fraction, we fail the audit, the partnership falls through, they lay off the junior staff to save money, and I'm out on the street because I can't pay my roommate." 

So the evaluation itself isn't really the trigger, if that makes sense? I don't care if they judge my technique. It's just another excuse for my brain to run through all the ways my life is going to fall apart. It doesn't feel any different or any more intense than when I'm sitting completely alone in my apartment on a Sunday night worrying about the exact same thing. The anxiety doesn't spike just because I'm being graded. It's just... it's always there, whether someone is holding a clipboard or not.
Have you ever felt anxious about the possibility of becoming anxious, even if you weren't actually having a panic attack or physical symptoms?

No, I don't think so. I mean, I don't really sit around worrying about getting anxious, because... well, I'm already anxious, you know? It's not like it's this separate event that I'm dreading might happen to me. It's just my baseline. It's like asking if I worry about breathing—I'm just doing it all the time. 

I guess what I'm trying to say is, I don't have this fear of the anxiety itself. The anxiety isn't the problem, in my head, at least. It's the things I'm anxious *about*. Like, I don't wake up and think, "Oh man, I hope I don't get really worried today about my job or my classes." I just wake up and immediately start worrying about my job and my classes. 

Like yesterday morning, for example. I didn't wake up dreading that I was going to feel anxious. I woke up, looked at the ceiling, and immediately thought about this email I sent to the lab manager on Friday. I started dissecting every word of it, wondering if I sounded too demanding when I asked for clarification on the new solvent disposal protocols. And then I started worrying that he's going to think I'm incompetent because I had to ask, and that's going to go in my file. I spent the whole morning chewing on that, right through my shower, right through making coffee. 

So the anxiety is just the vehicle, I guess. It's the lens I'm looking through. I'm not afraid of the lens; I'm afraid of what I'm seeing through it. I don't have this meta-anxiety where I'm anxious about being anxious. It's always attached to something real, something out there in the world that could actually go wrong and mess up my life. The fear is always about the consequences of the things I'm worrying about, not the act of worrying itself. It's just so constant that there's no room to worry about it starting, because it never really stops.

No, I don't think so. I mean, I don't really sit around worrying about getting anxious, because... well, I'm already anxious, you know? It's not like it's this separate event that I'm dreading might happen to me. It's just my baseline. It's like asking if I worry about breathing—I'm just doing it all the time. 

I guess what I'm trying to say is, I don't have this fear of the anxiety itself. The anxiety isn't the problem, in my head, at least. It's the things I'm anxious *about*. Like, I don't wake up and think, "Oh man, I hope I don't get really worried today about my job or my classes." I just wake up and immediately start worrying about my job and my classes. 

Like yesterday morning, for example. I didn't wake up dreading that I was going to feel anxious. I woke up, looked at the ceiling, and immediately thought about this email I sent to the lab manager on Friday. I started dissecting every word of it, wondering if I sounded too demanding when I asked for clarification on the new solvent disposal protocols. And then I started worrying that he's going to think I'm incompetent because I had to ask, and that's going to go in my file. I spent the whole morning chewing on that, right through my shower, right through making coffee. 

So the anxiety is just the vehicle, I guess. It's the lens I'm looking through. I'm not afraid of the lens; I'm afraid of what I'm seeing through it. I don't have this meta-anxiety where I'm anxious about being anxious. It's always attached to something real, something out there in the world that could actually go wrong and mess up my life. The fear is always about the consequences of the things I'm worrying about, not the act of worrying itself. It's just so constant that there's no room to worry about it starting, because it never really stops.

inference.note: The patient's anxiety remains persistent, generalized, and not tied to specific phobias, social situations, panic attacks, or obsessive-compulsive behaviors. The absence of physical symptoms during anxiety episodes, lack of panic attacks, and absence of compulsive behaviors or fear of anxiety itself further rule out other candidates such as F40.00, F40.10, F42.0, and F40.01. The anxiety is consistently tied to real-life concerns and pervasive across multiple domains, supporting a diagnosis of generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1).

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with excessive, persistent, and uncontrollable worry about multiple everyday events and responsibilities (e.g., job performance, finances, academic progress), occurring more days than not for at least six months. The anxiety is not limited to social situations or performance contexts, is not accompanied by physical panic attacks or compulsive behaviors, and lacks fear of anxiety itself or somatic symptoms typically associated with panic disorder. The cognitive focus of the anxiety and the chronic, free-floating nature of the worry align with generalized anxiety disorder (F41.1).
